rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid locates the stars in the sky and glosses their mawāqiʿ as their risings and settings.
rows.anchor: في السماء ويقال مطالعها ومساقطها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets the stars’ mawāqiʿ as their settings.
rows.anchor: {فلا أقسم بمواقع النجوم} [الواقعة: 75] «أي مساقطها»

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda also reports the interpretation that the oath is by the stars’ stations.
rows.anchor: {فلا أقسم بمواقع النجوم} [الواقعة: 75] قال: «بمنازل النجوم»

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the sites as the stars’ darkening and scattering on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: «انكدارها وانتثارها يوم القيامة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the stars’ setting and disappearance in the sky: mawqiʿ is the place or time of falling, its most evident sense here.
rows.anchor: معنى ذلك: فلا أقسم بمساقط النجوم ومغايبها في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufan readers mostly read the singular mawqiʿ; most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans read the plural mawāqiʿ. Both are recognized and equivalent.
rows.anchor: قرأته عامة قراء الكوفة (بموقع) على التوحيد، وقرأته عامة قراء المدينة والبصرة وبعض الكوفيين {بمواقع}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly life is temporary play, amusement, adornment, mutual boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children; like rain-grown greenery it becomes yellow after its fresh green growth.
rows.anchor: متاع الحياة الدنيا المعجلة لكم، ما هي إلا لعب ولهو تتفكهون به، وزينة تتزينون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plant dries and breaks into dry fragments; the afterlife holds severe punishment for disbelievers and forgiveness and favor for believers.
rows.anchor: يقول: «صار الناس إلى هذين الحرفين في الآخرة»

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says people ultimately come to these two outcomes in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: يقول: «صار الناس إلى هذين الحرفين في الآخرة»

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
rows.claim: A grammarian says the afterlife is either punishment or Paradise, and the conjunction wāw functions like aw, “or.”
rows.anchor: وأما الآخرة فإنها إما عذاب، وإما جنة قال: والواو فيه وأو بمنزلة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must fulfill God's obligations and avoid disobedience, then examine what deeds they sent ahead for Resurrection: saving good deeds or ruinous bad ones.
rows.anchor: ولينظر أحدكم ما قدم ليوم القيامة من الأعمال، أمن الصالحات التي تنجيه أم من السيئات التي توبقه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God made the Hour feel near by describing it as tomorrow, the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ما زال ربكم يقرب الساعة حتى جعلها كغد، وغد يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses “tomorrow” as the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: {ما قدمت لغد} [الحشر: 18] يعني يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise says “tomorrow” means the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: يقول في قوله: {ما قدمت لغد} [الحشر: 18] يعني يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says one should consider good and evil for the afterlife; yesterday denotes worldly life and tomorrow the afterlife, as in the image of a town gone by yesterday.
rows.anchor: يعني يوم القيامة الخير والشر؛ قال: والأمس في الدنيا، وغد في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children must not cause believers to neglect remembrance of God; the verb means to distract or divert someone from something.
rows.anchor: ألهيته عن كذا وكذا، فلها هو يلهو لهوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb’s meaning is illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays’s line about distracting a woman from her child with amulets.
rows.anchor: ومثلك حبلى قد طرقت ومرضع … فألهيتها عن ذي تمائم محول

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk interprets remembrance of God here specifically as the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: قال: الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should spend before death; the dying person asks for a brief reprieve to give alms and obey God by fulfilling obligations.
rows.anchor: يقول: فأزكي مالي {وأكن من الصالحين} [المنافقون: 10] يقول: وأعمل بطاعتك، وأؤدي فرائضك

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Another interpretation of becoming righteous is to perform the pilgrimage to the Sacred House.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عنى بقوله: {وأكن من الصالحين} [المنافقون: 10] وأحج بيتك الحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a person who dies without paying zakat or performing Hajj asks to return; he reads “give alms” as zakat and “be righteous” as Hajj.
rows.anchor: ما من أحد يموت ولم يؤد زكاة ماله ولم يحج إلا سأل الكرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Hajj is due when one has a mount to carry them and provisions to get there.
rows.anchor: قال: راحلة تحمله، ونفقة تبلغه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk describes a believer dying with wealth but unpaid zakat, unperformed Hajj, and unpaid dues to God; he asks to return, but death is not delayed.
rows.anchor: هو الرجل المؤمن نزل به الموت وله مال كثير لم يزكه، ولم يحج منه، ولم يعط منه حق الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās similarly says such a believer asks to return in order to give charity and zakat before the appointed death.
rows.anchor: هو الرجل المؤمن إذا نزل به الموت وله مال لم يزكه ولم يحج منه

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān glosses the requested alms and righteousness as zakat and Hajj.
rows.anchor: {فأصدق وأكن من الصالحين} [المنافقون: 10] قال: الزكاة والحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most regional readers recite wa-akun with jussive mood, coordinated with the implied jussive after fa-asaddaq; Ibn Muḥayṣin and Abū ʿAmr read wa-akūna in the subjunctive, coordinated with the subjunctive fa-asaddaq. Both readings are valid.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ذلك عامة قراء أهل الأمصار غير ابن محيصن وأبي عمرو: {وأكن} [يوسف: 33] جزما

none: only a sentence-ending continuation word appears in this segment body

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers all creatures for judgment; that day is mutual loss, as the people of Paradise gain against the people of Hell.
rows.anchor: قال: هو غبن أهل الجنة أهل النار

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains the Day of Mutual Loss as the people of Paradise gaining over the people of Hell.
rows.anchor: هو يوم القيامة، وهو يوم التغابن: يوم غبن أهل الجنة أهل النار

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the gathering and mutual-loss day is the Day of Resurrection, when Paradise's people gain over Hell's.
rows.anchor: هو يوم القيامة، وهو يوم التغابن: يوم غبن أهل الجنة أهل النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls it one of the names of Resurrection, magnified by God as a warning to His servants.
rows.anchor: من أسماء يوم القيامة، عظمه وحذره عباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever believes in God, obeys His commands, and avoids His prohibitions has sins erased and enters gardens with rivers below, remaining there forever; this is the great triumph.
rows.anchor: يقول: ويدخله بساتين تجري من تحت أشجارها الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man must house his divorced wife for her waiting period according to his means; the verse's wajd means the capacity one can find.
rows.anchor: وإنما أمر الرجال أن يعطوهن مسكنا يسكنه مما يجدونه، حتى يقضين عددهن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses wajd as one's means.
rows.anchor: {أسكنوهن من حيث سكنتم من وجدكم} [الطلاق: 6] يقول: من سعتكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid likewise defines wajd as means or capacity.
rows.anchor: {من وجدكم} [الطلاق: 6] قال: من سعتكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says to house her according to one's means, even in a corner of one's own home if that is all one has.
rows.anchor: فإن لم تجد إلا ناحية بيتك فأسكنها فيه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the husband must house and maintain a woman he divorces.
rows.anchor: المرأة يطلقها، فعليه أن يسكنها، وينفق عليها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says housing is owed according to ability: a man with means must keep her housed, including paying rent if able, whereas inability to secure housing excuses him.
rows.anchor: وإذا كان به قوة على الكراء فذاك وجده، لا يخرجها من منزلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A well-off former husband pays from his means for his ex-wife's nursing and their young child; a man with restricted provision pays according to what God gave him.
rows.anchor: فلم يوسع عليه، فلينفق مما أعطاه الله على قدر ماله

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī glosses ample means as one's available wealth and constrained provision as being given little.
rows.anchor: قال: من سعة موجده، قال: {ومن قدر عليه رزقه} [الطلاق: 7] قال: من قتر عليه رزقه

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān explains spending from one's means as spending according to one's capacity.
rows.anchor: {لينفق ذو سعة من سعته} [الطلاق: 7] يقول: من طاقته

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the required payment is set according to what the man can find.
rows.anchor: قال: فرض لها من قدر ما يجد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the spending is owed to the divorced woman if she nurses the man's child.
rows.anchor: {لينفق ذو سعة من سعته} [الطلاق: 7] قال: على المطلقة إذا أرضعت له

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar sent Abū ʿUbayda a thousand dinars and, after he used them for finer clothes and food, said he had rightly applied the verse on spending according to means.
rows.anchor: رحمه الله تأول هذه الآية {لينفق ذو سعة من سعته ومن قدر عليه رزقه فلينفق مما آتاه الله}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God requires spending on dependents only within the provision He has given, according to each person's means; the poor are not held to the rich person's obligation.
rows.anchor: لا يكلف الفقير مثل ما يكلف الغني

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says God does not charge the poor with the same burden as the rich.
rows.anchor: قال: يقول: لا يكلف الفقير مثل ما يكلف الغني

rows.speaker: هشيم
rows.claim: Hushaym glosses God's limit as what He has made obligatory.
rows.anchor: قال: إلا ما افترض عليها

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān interprets the limit as what a person can afford.
rows.anchor: يقول: إلا ما أطاقت

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God does not demand charity or zakat from someone who has nothing to give or purify.
rows.anchor: لا يكلفه الله أن يتصدق وليس عنده ما يتصدق به، ولا يكلفه الله أن يزكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tested the Quraysh disbelievers as He tested the garden owners: they swore to harvest at dawn and did not say “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: فأقسموا ليصرمنها مصبحين، ولا يستثنون

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the owners were Ethiopians whose father fed the poor from his garden; after he died, his sons called him foolish and vowed to exclude the poor.
rows.anchor: هم ناس من الحبشة كانت لأبيهم جنة كان يطعم المساكين منها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the garden belonged to a charitable old man; his sons opposed his charity and, after his death, set out to keep poor people away.
rows.anchor: كانت الجنة لشيخ، وكان يتصدق، فكان بنوه ينهونه عن الصدقة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the garden owners were People of the Book.
rows.anchor: كانوا من أهل الكتاب والصرم: القطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root ṣ-r-m means cutting; here they intended to gather or pick the garden's fruit.
rows.anchor: وإنما عنى بقوله: {ليصرمنها} [القلم: 17] ليجدن ثمرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays's line uses ṣaram for cutting off or severing a relationship, illustrating the root's meaning.
rows.anchor: والصرم: القطع، وإنما عنى بقوله: {ليصرمنها} [القلم: 17] ليجدن ثمرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A divine visitor struck the garden while its owners slept; in Arabic a ṭāʾif ordinarily comes at night, though one may explicitly say it came by day.
rows.anchor: طاف عليها أمر من أمر الله وهم نائمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites Abū al-Jarrāḥ's verse saying “I visited it by day, not at night,” showing that daytime visitation can be stated explicitly.
rows.anchor: أطفت بها نهارا غير ليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes the destructive visitor as an act or command from God.
rows.anchor: هو أمر من أمر الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses ṣarīm as night.
rows.anchor: {فأصبحت كالصريم} [القلم: 20] قال: الصريم: الليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that ṣarīm means night, a view illustrated by the poetry cited in the heading.
rows.anchor: {فأصبحت كالصريم} [القلم: 20] قال: الصريم: الليل

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Another view says al-Ṣarīm was a known place, a Yemeni land called Ḍarwān near Ṣanʿāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: بل معنى ذلك: فأصبحت كأرض تدعى الصريم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says al-Ṣarīm was a known place in Yemen called Ḍarwān, six miles from Ṣanʿāʾ.
rows.anchor: هي أرض باليمن يقال لها ضروان من صنعاء على ستة أميال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owners called to one another in the morning to head to their crop if they meant to harvest it, then whispered together to prevent any poor person from entering the garden.
rows.anchor: يقول: وهم يتسارون يقول بعضهم لبعض: لا يدخلن جنتكم اليوم عليكم مسكين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses their takhāfut as keeping their talk secret.
rows.anchor: يقول: يسرون {أن لا يدخلنها اليوم عليكم مسكين} [القلم: 24]

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the sons set out after their father died, resolved to exclude the poor.
rows.anchor: لما مات أبوهم غدوا عليها، فقالوا: لا يدخلنها اليوم عليكم مسكين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads ḥard as having ability or power within themselves.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وغدوا على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: ذوي قدرة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they went with seriousness and felt able to carry out their plan.
rows.anchor: في قول الله: {على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: على جد قادرين في أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan glosses ḥard as effort or seriousness.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {وغدوا على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: على جهد، أو قال على جد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they hurried toward their garden, confident in their ability.
rows.anchor: غدا القوم وهم محردون إلى جنتهم، قادرون عليها في أنفسهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd likewise interprets ḥard as serious purpose and confidence in their ability.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] على جد قادرين في أنفسهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the brothers shared their father’s crop and resolved not to feed the poor until they knew its yield.
rows.anchor: قال: كان حرث لأبيهم، وكانوا إخوة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they had already settled on their plan together.
rows.anchor: لا نطعم مسكينا منه حتى نعلم ما يخرج منه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid also glosses ḥard as a matter settled by agreement.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {على حرد} [القلم: 25] قال: على أمر مجمع

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima likewise interprets ḥard as an agreed and settled plan.
rows.anchor: {وغدوا على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: على أمر مجمع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan offers poverty or need as another meaning of ḥard.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن، في قوله: {وغدوا على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: على فاقة

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān reads ḥard as anger and cites Ashhab ibn Rumayla’s verse about two lions drinking blood in anger.
rows.anchor: عن سفيان، {وغدوا على حرد قادرين} [القلم: 25] قال: على حنق

rows.speaker: بعض أهل المعرفة بكلام العرب
rows.claim: Some Basran specialists suggest ḥard means withholding, connecting it with a rainless year or a camel without milk.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض أهل المعرفة بكلام العرب من أهل البصرة يتأول ذلك: وغدوا على منع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the withholding interpretation has no known early authority, although it has a possible linguistic basis.
rows.anchor: لا نعلم له قائلا من متقدمي العلم قاله وإن كان له وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers that they went toward the garden with an agreed, intended, concealed plan, capable in their own estimation; ḥard commonly means to aim toward something.
rows.anchor: يعني: يقصد قصدها، صح أن الذي هو أولى بتأويل الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rajaz line uses ḥarada for heading toward a destination, supporting the preferred sense of deliberate purpose.
rows.anchor: كان من أمر الله … يحرد حرد الجنة المغلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some brothers first think they lost the way; another recognizes their own garden and says its benefit has been denied them.
rows.anchor: أغفلوا طريق جنتهم، وأن التي رأوا غيرها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they thought they had taken the wrong path.
rows.anchor: {فلما رأوها قالوا إنا لضالون} [القلم: 26] أي ضللنا الطريق

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they had been repaid by being deprived of their garden.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: {بل نحن محرومون} [القلم: 27] حرمنا جنتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden’s owners were deprived of its benefit when its crop was destroyed.
rows.anchor: حرمنا منفعة جنتنا بذهاب حرثها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī takes awsaṭuhum to mean the most just or best; Ibn ʿAbbās links “middle” with justice in 2:143.
rows.anchor: قال: أعدلهم، ويقال: قال خيرهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the middle brother as the most just.
rows.anchor: قوله {قال أوسطهم} [القلم: 28] يقول: أعدلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses the middle brother as the most just.
rows.anchor: {قال أوسطهم} [القلم: 28] أعدلهم

rows.speaker: سعيد
rows.claim: Saʿīd also says he was the most just.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد، {قال أوسطهم} [القلم: 28] قال: أعدلهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda calls him the fairest in speech, quickest to fear, and best to turn back in repentance.
rows.anchor: أي أعدلهم قولا، وكان أسرع القوم فزعا، وأحسنهم رجعة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise glosses him as the most just.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {قال أوسطهم} [القلم: 28] يقول: أعدلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explicitly glosses tasbīḥ as making an exception; among these people, glorification meant saying “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: يقول: تستثنون، فكان التسبيح فيهم الاستثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human described is the disbeliever, created with intense anxiety: extreme panic combined with greed, impatience, and frustration.
rows.anchor: يقول تعالى ذكره: إن الإنسان الكافر خلق هلوعا والهلع: شدة الجزع مع شدة الحرص والضجر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the person as the one who panics when harmed and withholds when given good, and says this describes associators.
rows.anchor: قال: هو الذي قال الله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses halūʿ as miserly and panic-stricken.
rows.anchor: عن جعفر بن أبي المغيرة، عن سعيد بن جبير، {إن الإنسان خلق هلوعا} [المعارج: 19] قال: شحيحا جزوعا

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima defines halūʿ as fretful or easily vexed.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة، {إن الإنسان خلق هلوعا} [المعارج: 19] قال: ضجورا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the disbeliever is stingy and withholds good, panicking when misfortune strikes.
rows.anchor: هو بخيل منوع للخير، جزوع إذا نزل به البلاء

rows.speaker: حصين
rows.claim: Ḥuṣayn glosses halūʿ as greedy or covetous.
rows.anchor: سألت حصينا عن هذه الآية: {إن الإنسان خلق هلوعا}

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses halūʿ as panic-stricken.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {إن الإنسان خلق هلوعا} [المعارج: 19] قال: الهلوع: الجزوع

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda likewise says halūʿ means panic-stricken.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {خلق هلوعا} [المعارج: 19] قال: جزوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one among creation can protect or help the Prophet from God if God intends something for him.
rows.anchor: إنما يريد محمد أن نجيره، وأنا أجيره فأنزل الله

rows.speaker: حضرمي
rows.claim: A report says a prominent jinn declared he would protect Muhammad, after which this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: إنما يريد محمد أن نجيره، وأنا أجيره فأنزل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multaḥad means a refuge or shelter to which one might flee from God.
rows.anchor: يقول: ولن أجد من دون الله ملجأ ألجأ إليه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses it as a refuge and helper.
rows.anchor: أي ملجأ ونصيرا

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān also interprets it as a refuge or supporter.
rows.anchor: يقول: ناصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food will stick in the eater's throat: it neither goes down nor comes back out.
rows.anchor: شوك يأخذ بالحلق، فلا يدخل ولا يخرج

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says it is a thorn that catches in the throat and can neither enter nor exit.
rows.anchor: قال: شوك يأخذ بالحلق، فلا يدخل ولا يخرج

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the choking food as the tree of Zaqqūm.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وطعاما ذا غصة} [المزمل: 13] قال: شجرة الزقوم

rows.speaker: حمران بن أعين
rows.claim: Ḥumrān ibn Aʿyan reports that the Prophet recited the description of shackles, Hell, and choking food, then fainted; al-Ṭabarī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ: {إن لدينا أنكالا وجحيما وطعاما ذا غصة} [المزمل: 13] فصعق صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath refutes the claim that Hell's keepers would be enough to drive the Prophet's companions away; God swears by the moon and departing night.
rows.anchor: ليس القول كما يقول من زعم أنه يكفي أصحابه المشركين خزنة جهنم حتى يجهضهم عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night is described as departing and going away.
rows.anchor: والليل إذ ولى ذاهبا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses the night as having departed.
rows.anchor: {والليل إذ أدبر} [المدثر: 33] إذ ولى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās instead describes the night as darkening.
rows.anchor: دبوره: إظلامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most Medinan and Basran readers read idh adbara, while some Meccan and Kufan readers read idhā dabara; al-Ṭabarī accepts both as valid and equivalent dialect forms.
rows.anchor: أنهُما قراءتان معروفتان صحيحتا المعنى، فبأيتهما قرأ القارئ فمصيب

rows.speaker: بعض الكوفيين
rows.claim: Some Kufans call the forms dialectal pairs: dabbara/adbara and qabila/aqbala, while using the prefixed form for a rider's coming or going.
rows.anchor: هما لغتان، يقال: دبر النهار وأدبر، ودبر الصيف وأدبر

rows.speaker: بعض البصريين
rows.claim: Some Basrans say dabara means the day has passed and is at its end, while adbara means turned away; Al-Ṭabarī prefers that both readings mean the same and cites Arabic usage and interpreters' lack of distinction.
rows.anchor: والصواب من القول في ذلك عندي أنهما لغتان بمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The morning is brightening; Qatāda says it has become bright and is arriving.
rows.anchor: {والصبح إذا أسفر} [المدثر: 34] إذا أضاء وأقبل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses dawn as brightening and coming on.
rows.anchor: {والصبح إذا أسفر} [المدثر: 34] إذا أضاء وأقبل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the “greatest matters” as Hell.
rows.anchor: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] يعني: جهنم

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abū Razīn likewise says the reference is Hell.
rows.anchor: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] قال: جهنم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies it as the Fire.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] قال: هذه النار

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says it is the Fire.
rows.anchor: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] قال: هي النار

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it is Hell.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] يعني: جهنم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also says it is Hell.
rows.anchor: {إنها لإحدى الكبر} [المدثر: 35] يعني جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī first glosses “a warning to humankind” as Hell warning human beings; on this reading nadhīran is an accusative detached modifier of “one of the greatest.”
rows.anchor: والله ما أنذر الناس بشيء أدهى منها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says people were warned of no greater or more dreadful calamity than this.
rows.anchor: والله ما أنذر الناس بشيء أدهى منها

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abū Razīn takes God as the subject: God says He warns people of Hell so they should fear it.
rows.anchor: يقول الله: أنا لكم منها نذير فاتقوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical interpretation makes nadhīran an accusative verbal noun, “a warning,” outside the prior clause, or says the Fire was made one of the great matters as a warning.
rows.anchor: يقول الله: أنا لكم منها نذير فاتقوها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says “humankind” means the children of Adam and identifies Muhammad as the warner, with nadhīran construed as a circumstantial accusative after “arise.”
rows.anchor: قال: بنو آدم البشر، فقيل له: محمد النذير قال: نعم ينذرهم

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some interpreters say the unmentioned interval was forty years, when Adam's clay form had been fashioned but had not yet received a soul; he existed bodily but was not yet remembered.
rows.anchor: الإنسان حين من الدهر لم يكن شيئا مذكورا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the muʿṣirāt are winds.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وأنزلنا من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] فالمعصرات: الريح

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima's reading with bi- rather than min identifies the muʿṣirāt as winds.
rows.anchor: حدثنا ابن حميد، قال: ثنا يحيى بن واضح، قال: ثنا الحسين، عن يزيد، عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the muʿṣirāt are winds.
rows.anchor: قوله: {من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] قال: الريح

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says one reading has bi-l-maʿṣirāt, meaning the winds.
rows.anchor: في بعض القراءات: (وأنزلنا بالمعصرات)

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the muʿṣirāt as winds and cites the verse about winds raising clouds.
rows.anchor: قال: المعصرات: الرياح، وقرأ قول الله: {الذي يرسل الرياح فتثير سحابا}

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān interprets the muʿṣirāt as clouds.
rows.anchor: {من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] قال: المعصرات: السحاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise identifies them as clouds.
rows.anchor: {وأنزلنا من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] يقول: من السحاب

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says the muʿṣirāt are clouds.
rows.anchor: {المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] السحاب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the water descends from the sky.
rows.anchor: {وأنزلنا من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] قال: من السماء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda likewise says water is sent down from the heavens.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وأنزلنا من المعصرات} [النبأ: 14] قال: من السموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers rain-bearing clouds: the text says water comes “from” the muʿṣirāt, whereas winds contain no water and carry rain; clouds are the usual source of rain, even if sky is possible.
rows.anchor: والرياح لا ماء فيها فينزل منها، وإنما ينزل بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thajj means water pouring in a continuous succession, like the pouring of sacrificial blood.
rows.anchor: {ماء ثجاجا} [النبأ: 14] ماء من السماء منصبا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ gloss thajj as pouring; Sufyān says it comes successively.
rows.anchor: {ماء ثجاجا} [النبأ: 14] قال: منصبا

rows.speaker: ابن وهب
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says thajj means abundant, but al-Ṭabarī rejects this as unattested for quantity in Arabic and prefers continuous pouring, supported by the Prophetic phrase “the best Hajj is loud invocation and sacrifice.”
rows.anchor: {ماء ثجاجا} [النبأ: 14] قال: كثيرا ولا يعرف في كلام العرب من صفة الكثرة الثج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water produces grains, the seed-bearing kernels enclosed in husks and harvested, like barley grains and dates.
rows.anchor: تضمنه كمام الزرع التي تحصد، وهي جمع حبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabāt means fodder for grazing, including grasses and crops.
rows.anchor: وأما النبات فهو الكلأ الذي يرعى، من الحشيش والزروع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alfāfan means gardens densely entwined and gathered together; the early interpreters agree on this sense.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وجنات ألفافا} [النبأ: 16] قال: مجتمعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the gardens are gathered together, one intertwined with another.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وجنات ألفافا} [النبأ: 16] قال: مجتمعة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses alfāfan as intertwined.
rows.anchor: {وجنات ألفافا} [النبأ: 16] قال: ملتفة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the gardens are intertwined, one beside another.
rows.anchor: قال: التف بعضها إلى بعض

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd describes gardens interwoven, some over others.
rows.anchor: قال: هي الملتفة، بعضها فوق بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says alfāf is the plural of liff or lafīf, because interpreters agree it means intertwined; lafāʾ means thick, which does not itself imply intertwining except by interpreting it as density from entanglement.
rows.anchor: والصواب من القول في ذلك أن الألفاف جمع لف أو لفيف، وذلك أن أهل التأويل مجمعون على أن معناه: ملتفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Decision is the appointed day when God separates the earliest and latest generations by their deeds; the verse “day the Horn is blown” explains that appointed event.
rows.anchor: يفصل الله فيه بين الأولين والآخرين بأعمالهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The Prophet says the ṣūr is a horn.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، قال: " الصور: قرن

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets the ṣūr as creation or created beings.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {يوم ينفخ في الصور} [الأنعام: 73] والصور: الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Great Overwhelming Calamity engulfs every lesser horror with its immense terror; it is also a name for the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: قوله: {فإذا جاءت الطامة الكبرى} [النازعات: 34] من أسماء يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls it one of Resurrection's names, magnified by God as a warning to His servants.
rows.anchor: من أسماء يوم القيامة، عظمه الله وحذره عباده

rows.speaker: القاسم بن الوليد
rows.claim: Al-Qāsim ibn al-Walīd says the people of Paradise are led to Paradise and the people of Hell to Hell.
rows.anchor: قال: سيق أهل الجنة إلى الجنة، وأهل النار إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the calamity comes, people remember their worldly deeds, both good and evil; that is what they pursued.
rows.anchor: يوم يتذكر الإنسان ما عمل في الدنيا من خير وشر، وذلك سعيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the one who fears God, fulfills obligations, avoids sin, and restrains disliked desires has Paradise as the abode on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: فإن الجنة هي مأواه ومنزله يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For such a person, Paradise is the abode and residence on Resurrection Day; al-Ṭabarī refers to his earlier discussion of the same phrase in 55:46.
rows.anchor: فإن الجنة هي مأواه ومنزله يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers ask when the Resurrection will be established and appear; irsāʾ is like a ship coming to rest, meaning that the Hour's advent becomes manifest and fixed, like justice or truth standing.
rows.anchor: رسوها: قيامها؛ قال: وليس قيامها كقيام القائم، إنما هي كقولك: قد قام العدل، وقام الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet has no assigned role in determining the Hour or investigating its timing; its endpoint belongs to God.
rows.anchor: في أي شيء أنت من ذكر الساعة والبحث عن شأنها

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says people kept asking the Prophet about the Hour until the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: لم يزل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يسأل عن الساعة، حتى أنزل الله

rows.speaker: طارق بن شهاب
rows.claim: Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb says the Prophet continually mentioned the Hour until the warning passage was revealed.
rows.anchor: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يزال يذكر شأن الساعة حتى نزلت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says “its remembrance” means the Hour.
rows.anchor: قوله: {فيم أنت من ذكراها} [النازعات: 43] قال: الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Muḥayṣin read munadhdhir with nunation, making the Prophet a warner of whoever fears the Hour.
rows.anchor: بالتنوين، بمعنى: أنه منذر من يخشاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Muḥayṣin read munadhdhir with nunation, “a warner of whoever fears it”; the other regional readers annex it to “whoever,” “warner of those who fear it.” Both readings are accepted.
rows.anchor: فبأيتهما قرأ القارئ فمصيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On seeing the Hour, the deniers will feel they spent only an evening or its morning in worldly life; Arabs use morning and evening for the first and last parts of a day.
rows.anchor: فكذلك قوله: {إلا عشية أو ضحاها} [النازعات: 46] إنما معناها إلا آخر يوم أو أوله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says worldly life will seem brief in their eyes when they encounter the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقت الدنيا في أعين القوم حين عاينوا الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God swears by the night as it withdraws; Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also interpret it as departing.
rows.anchor: قوله: {والليل إذا عسعس} [التكوير: 17] يقول: إذا أدبر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Reports say ʿAlī recited the paired oath of night and dawn after dawn appeared, then said it was the time for Witr prayer.
rows.anchor: أين السائل عن الوتر؟ نعم ساعة الوتر هذه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid gives both senses for ʿasʿasa: the night coming on and its departure.
rows.anchor: قال: إقباله، ويقال: إدباره

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses ʿasʿasa as turning away, with dawn's breath beginning from the direction of sunrise.
rows.anchor: قال: عسعس: تولى، وقال: تنفس الصبح من هاهنا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the night covers people; ʿAṭiyya gestures toward the west for the night coming on.
rows.anchor: قال: إذا غشي الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the night withdrawing because dawn is arriving; Arabic uses both ʿasʿasa and saʿsaʿa for a night nearing its end, as shown by poems of Ruʾba and ʿAlqama.
rows.anchor: فكانوا يرون أن هذا البيت مصنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Arabic specialists say ʿasʿasa means night beginning and darkening, citing a line al-Farrāʾ says was likely fabricated.
rows.anchor: فكانوا يرون أن هذا البيت مصنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is by daylight as its brightness arrives and becomes clear.
rows.anchor: في قوله: {والصبح إذا تنفس} [التكوير: 18] قال: إذا نشأ

rows.speaker: سعيد
rows.claim: Saʿīd says dawn has risen or emerged.
rows.anchor: قال: إذا نشأ

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says dawn brightens and comes on.
rows.anchor: {والصبح إذا تنفس} [التكوير: 18] : إذا أضاء وأقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath pairs the departing day with the arriving night. Al-Ṭabarī prefers shafaq as the day as it recedes; in the legal timing of ʿIshāʾ, shafaq means redness, as he explains in his book on prayer.
rows.anchor: إن الله أقسم بالنهار مدبرا، والليل مقبلا

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العراق
rows.claim: Some Iraqi scholars define shafaq as the red glow; Mujāhid describes it as redness of the horizon.
rows.anchor: إن الشفق من الشمس، ولكن قل: حمرة الأفق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says shafaq is the whole day, and elsewhere describes it as the redness of the horizon.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، قوله: الشفق، قال: النهار كله

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Another view treats shafaq as the name for both red and white, making it a word with opposite senses.
rows.anchor: الشفق: هو اسم للحمرة والبياض، وقالوا: هو من الأضداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasq means gathering; the oath covers what night gathers among creatures that settle, fly, or crawl after daytime. The root also describes collected food in a container, and a wasq is sixty ṣāʿs.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وما وسق} [الانشقاق: 17] يقول: وما جمع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “what it gathers” as whatever night collects, and cites a poetic line about creatures crowded together if they had a herder.
rows.anchor: قوله: {وما وسق} [الانشقاق: 17] يقول: وما جمع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says it is whatever the night gathers or shelters, including creatures it contains; he also glosses the phrase as what it folds or covers.
rows.anchor: قال: وما جمع، يقول: ما آوى فيه من دابة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the night gathers stars or animals.
rows.anchor: يقول: وما جمع من نجم أو دابة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says it is whatever God gathers in the night: creatures that shelter there and things occurring at night but not during the day.
rows.anchor: مجتمع فيه الأشياء التي يجمعها الله، التي تأوي إليه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid also glosses wasaq as what entered the night or what it covered and drew together.
rows.anchor: قال: وما دخل فيه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says it is whatever the night gathers.
rows.anchor: {والليل وما وسق} [الانشقاق: 17] : وما جمع

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says it is what night encloses, or what it drives as darkness and sends each thing toward its shelter.
rows.anchor: قال: ما ساق من ظلمة، فإذا كان الليل، ذهب كل شيء إلى مأواه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the night brings darkness along as it arrives.
rows.anchor: قال: ما ساق معه من ظلمة إذا أقبل
